Lightning Round

Answer each of the following questions with one sentence including a brief explanation.

1. Finish the sentence with another student's name: "If [Name of Student] doesn't earn an A, then nobody should, because..."

If Jared Hammett doesn't earn an A, then nobody should, because he consistently provided the most thoughtful peer reviews going beyond pointing out errors to explaining why alternative approaches would be better.  

2. What was the most difficult part of the class for you? List a general topic, a specific problem, a kind of work we did, etc. and explain why.

The most difficult part of the class for me was understanding tidy evaluation and the curly-curly operator ({{ }}) in Lab 8, because it required a different type of thinking that I was not familiar with. The distinction between quoted and unquoted variable names felt completely backwards from everything I'd learned about programming before.

3. What was the easiest part of the class for you? Explain why.

The easiest part of the class for me was creating basic visualizations with ggplot2 in the beginning of the quarter. I had experience making plots and using basic R functions in my previous classes, so I was already familiar with the package and syntax.  

4. What part of the class surprised or interested you the most? Explain why.

I really enjoyed learning about the stylistic capabilities of R. I loved playing around with styling my Quarto docs and being able to create custom plots and tables. I also enjoyed improving my function writing skills; I knew how to write functions in python and java, but it was cool to learn function syntax in R. 

5. Give one piece of advice to a student just beginning a quarter of STAT 331 that will help them be successful in learning.

Start the assignments early and embrace getting stuck, because the most valuable learning happens when you're lost and then all of sudden find the correct code in lecture material or pre-class reading. You'll learn more from figuring out why fct_reorder2() produces a weird legend order than from breezing through ten assignments that work perfectly the first time, and giving yourself time to struggle (and ask for help when truly stuck) is what transforms you from someone who can follow examples to someone who can solve problems.
